utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is Tuesday, January 15, 2008, and I welcome everyone in the courtroom, people from the Prosecution, Mr. Seselj, and all those helping us. So first and foremost I would like to tell Mr. Seselj, maybe he already knows this, maybe he doesn't, that the panel of three Judges appointed by the President has decided to dismiss the Prosecution's motion. Yesterday the President gave an order regarding this dismissal. The procedure thus stands as it is and we can now go on. Mr. Seselj, you will obtain in your own language translation of this decision that was drafted in English. It was filed yesterday in the evening, so -- which is why it could be translated overnight. But I -- you know now exactly what this order is about. The motion is dismissed and Judge Harhoff is on the Bench and stays on the Bench. Before we bring the witness into the courtroom I have four items to discuss. I would like Mr. Seselj to listen carefully because this deals with documents that he sent to the Trial Chamber. Firstly, document 334 drafted by Mr. Seselj on November 2nd, 2007, and filed on November 8, 2008 [as interpreted]. In this document the accused was answering the notice -- the notice sent by the Prosecution regarding the order of the witnesses. The order of the witnesses has been changed since then, and this is why motion 334 is now moot. Secondly, document 350, this was drafted by Mr. Seselj on December 4, 2007, and filed on December 10, 2007. On December 4, 2007, Mr. Seselj was raising the following items in this document -- was raising several documents -- several items, and the Chamber -- the Trial Chamber will not deal with the two first items that have to do with protected witness. But regarding item number 3, the Trial Chamber would like to give its position, regarding the disclosure of possibly exculpatory documents, exhibits, according to Rule 68. On November 5, 2007, in its second decision dealing with requirements of Prosecution under Rule 68, the Chamber had ordered as follows, and I will quote this decision and I will read slowly: "Prosecution must disclose as quickly as possible in hard copy and in a language understood by the witness [as interpreted] the -- some 3.000 documents that Prosecution has identified using key words given by the accused." Therefore, in the submission 350, Mr. Seselj submits that Prosecution did not meet its requirement under this decision, since a great number of documents have not been translated into Serbian and since other documents are only excerpts. The Trial Chamber is thus asking Prosecution to reply on this point in writing, make a written submission, before Friday, January 18. Thirdly, dealing with document 358, document 358 was drafted on December 11, 2007, by Mr. Seselj and filed on February 2nd, 2008. In document 358 Mr. Seselj was asking leave for the ex parte status to be lifted regarding all documents and all appendices produced by Prosecution. The very general nature of this -- of submission 358 makes it impossible for the Trial Chamber at the moment to examine the merits of this submission. Trial Chamber would like to underscore that it is not up to the Trial Chamber to look into all the documents and to search all these documents to try and find out those who were disclosed to the accused and those who were not disclosed to the accused. It is up to the accused to be very precise and accurate in his submission. The Trial Chamber is thus asking Mr. Seselj to make a more accurate submission regarding what it is complaining about. And Mr. Seselj should just therefore give us his observations before January 18. Fourthly, and this item deals with the witness that we are about to hear, Trial Chamber is recalling its decision of January 1st -- January 7th, 2008, on the consolidated motion. It dismissed the Prosecution's request requesting the written statement to -- of this witness to be admitted according to Rule 92 ter, which is why the witness that we're about to hear will testify viva voce and not testify according to Rule 92 ter. These were the four points that I wanted to cover. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would just like to present a few problems with the wish of having these problems resolved before the next witnesses come in. It is not a problem related to this particular witness but to the one coming right after this witness, and I'm referring to the period of the next few weeks. The next witness is VS-004, the witness after this one, that is. I received his statement dated the 14th of August, 2006. That is an abbreviated version of the statement given on the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, and 4th of May, 2002; however, I received that one in redacted form. You see how many blackened portions there are there. I never received that statement in its entirety. You see, an entire page, for instance. I require the entire statement so that I can prepare properly for examining witness VS-004 and I want to get that as soon as possible. Also, you told me that you rejected lifting the seal from the documents submitted by the Government of the Republic of Serbia in relation to the documents that the OTP received from the current state security agency. It is document 426 -- it is 426 documents that are in question. I want the Prosecution to submit all these documents to me as soon as possible. I want to have a set of these documents in its entirety so that I could prepare for a public hearing that would be attended by a representative of the Government of Serbia. I oppose having a seal of confidentiality on these documents. They can be very important for me because they say what kind of measures the regime in Serbia applied towards me personally and the Serb Radical Party in 1991, 1992, and 1993, that is to say, the time relevant to the indictment. Therefore, it is impossible that I was in some kind of a joint criminal enterprise with the top people of that regime. On the one hand they are working against me and on the other hand I am in a joint criminal enterprise with them. I also want to tell you that a few days ago I was threatened by the Registrar that new restrictive measures would be imposed on me because my congratulations sent to Vladimir Putin was published in the Belgrade newspaper Pravda and I congratulated him on the victory of his party in the elections held in Russia. So please prevent the Registrar from doing that. I don't have a fax here on the premises, so can I please receive during breaks, during the course of the day, documents from my associates. Today it is indispensable for me to receive some 20 or 30 documents from my associates around 10.00, so could you please instruct the guards to take me to an office in this building where I can receive these documents by fax. There is no other way of doing this. For January and February the OTP announced 16 witnesses. Eight of them are Defence witnesses and they are not going to respond to Prosecution summons unless you bring them in by force.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note that the speaker should speak slower.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One witness died in September 2007. How are they going to organize that? Perhaps they're going to organize it via videolink. I have a introduce a note of black humour because obviously, the Prosecution does not even know that that witness died. The Prosecution informed me that they would raise that on the session of the 8th of November, that is to say that some documents in relation to Rule 65 ter should be admitted directly into evidence. First I got a list of these documents and then the documents themselves. I prepared myself for that session, I brought five boxes of these documents here, you may remember, the guards were carrying all of that behind me; however, nothing came out of it, this did not happen on the 8th. I want to rule out any possibility of having these documents admitted without me stating my views, and I have to state my views in a public session. I will not have any objections in relation to some documents, but I will have objections in relation to others. I also want to say something about Reynaud Theunens, an expert witness who is supposed to testify. Two hours were planned by the Prosecution for him, whereas I will require five hours. I will require five hours for re-examination because his expert report is 400 pages; that is very important for me, that is a very important Prosecution witness for me. So I ask you in advance that you give me that time and then you can take it off other witnesses' time. You will have other witnesses that will not come and also the witness who's dead, so you can save time there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mrs. Dahl maybe would like to answer quickly. There were six items that were mentioned --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Seven I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... immediately. The question of the faxes your associates will send around 10.30. I believe that your associates have a fax number and the fax will come to the Tribunal and registrar will bring you these documents over the break. So normally you should not have any problems with this -- have with this fax communication with your associates. There are two other items that did not call for any comments by the Prosecution. You talked about restrictive measures in your mentioning your congratulations to Vladimir Putin. It is true that I read this in your submissions. I'm a bit surprised this led to problems. After all, you're entitled to send your greetings to whoever you want. I do not really understand the registry's position. Of course the Trial Chamber will look into this. Now, regarding the other items, I'm sure Mrs. Dahl has an opinion. Mrs. Dahl, would you like to take the floor?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I will take them in the order that the accused raised them. I will look into the question regarding redactions in the witness statement of VS-004. I will note that the decision rejecting the motion pursuant to 89(F), 92 bis, 92 ter, and 92 quater requires a wholesale revision of the Prosecution's estimates on how to present its case and the number of hours that would be required for each witness. We are looking at the effect of the decision, including the invitation to resubmit applications in respect of identified witnesses. I would note that the Prosecution's estimates regarding the time required to present its case were uniformly based on the anticipation that we would have the ability to tender evidence in writing that was adopted by the witnesses pursuant to the Rules. Yesterday we filed a request with the Chamber to enlarge the time in which we may seek certification for leave to appeal. One of the bases for that request was rendered moot by the rejection of the application under Rule 15. The other basis is to avoid a piecemeal litigation because the decision pronounces that it is not final. There are other applications for which the Chamber is waiting to rule based on anticipated responses from the accused. So we would like to wait to make our application for certification to appeal the decision until we have a final order that disposes of all the matters in a consolidated manner. I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Dahl, yes, could you please tell us exactly, have I listened to you and I'm a bit lost. I don't understand. We rendered a decision regarding your motions 89(F), 92 bis, 92 ter, and 92 quater. A decision has been rendered on this. So either this decision suits you; or if it doesn't suit you, ask for a certification of appeal, that's one thing. Okay. Secondly, you are saying that this decision will have consequences on the time needed for -- to present your case, and therefore either you have or you are going to submit a motion for additional time. Well, the Trial Chamber did not get this. Of course the Trial Chamber will render its decision on this and of course you will be allowed here to request a certification of appeal. So you've -- when you mentioned this certification of appeal, what did it deal with exactly, could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What I filed yesterday was a motion for extension of time because I considered that it would be prudent to await the final disposition of the remaining items because the decision itself says that it's not final, that there is more judicial work to be done. We haven't requested more time to enlarge the presentation of the Prosecution's case consequent upon this decision because we need to take it under advisement and look at the case as a whole to see how it would affect the witnesses. With regard to the witness today, I anticipate that I'll need more than the four hours I've already estimated, but we had made all of our estimates based on the ability to put most of our evidence in in dossier format, meaning in writing, under the procedures available under the Rules. Does that answer your question sufficiently?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Somewhat, yet thank you. Could you please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Consequent upon the decision, we will be adjusting the time we need to examine Mr. Theunens' report. I don't have any objection to enlarging the time that Mr. Seselj needs to cross-examine him. I don't have a response to his request for the set of the documents, a specific set of the documents from the Republic of Serbia. My understanding is that we've already completely disclosed all of those materials. I'll need to research that because I'm not exactly sure what he's asking for, and if Mr. Seselj has information to which the Prosecution is not privy regarding the death of a witness, I'd kindly ask him to inform us so that we avoid wasting time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I will prepare a new production schedule now that we're back in session to try to confirm witnesses' availabilities. Mr. VS-004 was available to testify last week. I need to put into place a new production schedule with the witnesses updated. We had subpoenaed two witnesses to appear the first week in January, as the Court is aware, they sent -- the memorandum of service indicates that they wish safe conduct orders. I filed motions for those to resolve that concern and make it possible for them to travel. The remainder of their requests are not within the policy and protocol of the Tribunal. I conferred with the Victims and Witnesses Section and understand that none of the requests by the witnesses can be satisfied. I don't think that they prevent enforcement of the subpoena and I would request the Chamber to issue a ruling on the safe conduct orders so that we can then enforce the subpoenas as quickly as possible and give those witnesses a new appearance date and make the travel arrangements that are necessary. Finally, I want to ask the Chamber to please address the use of the DVDs that the accused receives at the conclusion of every session. They are posted on Mr. Seselj's web site. That in itself does not present any problems. My concern is that if we go into closed session that he is not permitted to distribute those disks or publish them on the web site, and I don't want to find out about this problem, frankly, in arrears. I would like to make sure this doesn't happen in advance. It's not for a legitimate investigative purpose to disclose these CDs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, let me immediately ask you this. I am discovering that there is this new problem and I did not know about it. The DVDs of the hearings, everything that is recorded here, are disclosed to you. It seems that you have a web site and everything is posted on the web site, but then we run into a huge problem. When we have a closed hearing it is totally impossible to publish or make public what was said in closed session. So what exactly do you do in this respect, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It happens, Mr. President, that Madam Dahl invents a problem sometimes, perhaps due to idleness. I receive a DVD with the recording of the entire proceedings. Apart from the DVD from the beginning of the trial, the opening statement of the Prosecution and my own statement, I have not had time to send a single DVD to Belgrade; they're still in my cell. Never have I placed any of the DVDs received from the registry on my internet web site. My collaborators in Belgrade post on my web site exclusively recordings broadcast on Serbian State Television. I don't know whether you're aware that the Serbian State Television gave the recording of the beginning of the trial and Anton Oberschall's statement or testimony, it was broadcast after 10.00 p.m. My collaborators take this from the TV and put it on my web site. Madam Dahl is creating a problem where there is no problem because I have never broadcast a single tiny little part of any closed session. Secondly, as for the other issues raised by Madam Dahl, may I state what I think of them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, if you have a DVD with part of the recording that was in closed session, you will not disclose this to the public, you will not make it public, right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not a child, Judge. Why would I deny myself certain rights in these proceedings by violating certain prohibitions? The only people I give this to is -- are my collaborators, and it will not be broadcast anywhere unless a protective measure is abolished. The only recordings broadcast on my internet site are those from the state television of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This is very clear. So what else did you want to say as a reply?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for what Madam Dahl has said, I have received the text of the Prosecution motion for safe conduct, but I'm waiting for the Chamber to hand down its decision concerning the objection raised by the witnesses who have been issued by -- with a subpoena by you. They have stated that they are my witnesses, not Prosecution witnesses. If you force them to come, they will come, they won't flee; but if they come, if they're coerced into coming, they will continue to behave as Defence witnesses and they will refuse any contact or conversation with the OTP. These are witnesses that were interviewed a long time ago by the OTP as potential suspects, and that is the capacity in which they made their statements. I have not received the transcript of a single one of these interviews. They have to be disclosed to me but they haven't been disclosed. These people do not wish to be Prosecution witnesses; they want to testify as my witnesses, and they have stated that explicitly. They speak out in public in Serbia. I will not mention their names because here they are considered to be protected witnesses, but they have made statements for the newspapers. They have certified in court their statements that they do not wish to be Prosecution witnesses but Defence witnesses. The issue now is whether you will allow them to appear here as Prosecution -- as Defence witnesses. In 2005 I contacted VS-011, and he gave me part of his interview with the OTP and I published this in my book entitled: "The Devil's Disciple, the Criminal Pope, John Paul II." He gave that to me and I published it. I had no idea at the time that the Prosecution was counting on him as a Prosecution witness. His name was disclosed to me at the end of last year, two years after that event, up until that time I had already agreed with him that he would appear here as a Defence witness. The case of the others is similar, so don't allow the Prosecution to take these witnesses away from me. As for the Serbian government statement, it's true that the Prosecution disclosed to me some of these statements but not all. There are 426 documents in total and there -- the list of these documents is in two parts. The motion of the Government of Serbia has two annexes, one containing 27 documents and the other one 399. I want to receive the entire set of these documents before there is a discussion on the Serbian government motion. These documents are extremely important to me. Some of them are supposed to prove criminal conduct of mine, alleged criminal conduct, but no Court can accept this as evidence anywhere, in Italy, in Denmark, or anywhere, and they cannot be considered evidence under an Anglo-Saxon law either, but they are important to me because they show that the regime used repressive measures against me and my collaborators in 1991, 1992, 1993, in all the years relevant for the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Out of the 426 documents, the Trial Chamber has been seized as to the issue of confidentiality of the documents. We shall issue a decision, but that's not the urgent problem. The urgent problem seems to be that there is a first batch of 27 documents and a second batch of 399 documents. Mr. Seselj wants to have them, and you said that you had disclosed them to you, I don't know. Did you give it all? You are the only one to know.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, we gave Mr. Seselj copies of the documents we intend to use as evidence in this case. As far as I'm aware, this is his first request to review all of them and I would treat that as a request for disclosure under Rule 66 and proceed accordingly. I don't see any impediment to ruling on a request to add that subset of documents to our exhibit list. I would like to go into private session for a moment to discuss one remaining issue concerning a confidential filing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are now in private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj has made a motion to investigate me under Rule 77 for contempt. I would like direction from the Chamber whether the Prosecution should file a response or not. I don't presently see an impediment to me continuing to lead the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is indeed a motion that has been filed against you. The Trial Chamber is going to hand down a decision. You are free to file a response if you wish to, no problem to that. We are going to issue a decision, that goes without saying. For the time being you are present here, but you are free to answer, to respond to the filing by Mr. Seselj if you wish to, but you have to do so quickly if you want to because we are to issue this decision shortly. Let's move back to open session, please, and we're going to have the witness brought in. Open session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, I only wish to submit a motion to the Trial Chamber for this closed session or private session to be declared public because there's nothing in there that the public is not supposed to know. The fact that I submitted a criminal report against Madam Dahl is public. Not a single detail has been mentioned here that should be concealed from the public, so I move that this part of the proceedings be made public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not getting any English interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I repeat. You had initially four hours for this witness. Earlier on you said you needed an extension of time. How much more time do you want?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it would take me eight hours to go through the documents we had foreseen and the full breadth of the witness statement. If I can use the time today and give you a better estimate tomorrow. There's a lot of detailed information in the statement we had foreseen to tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll see. We'll see how it all unfolds, because if you're given eight hours that means that Mr. Seselj is going to be given eight hours as well. So the witness would stay here basically next week as well. So that's the situation as we find it. I don't know at all this witness. I don't know at all how the situation is going to unfold. So we'll see as we go along. Let's have the witness brought in for the solemn declaration, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. Let me first check that you can hear me in your own language. If you hear the interpretation say, I understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You're going to make the solemn declaration. You need to stand up to do so. For the transcript could you please state your name, first name and date of birth. One moment, please. Before, you have to give your name, your first name and your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Goran Stoparic, the 17th of January, 1968.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have a current occupation or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have my own company, my enterprise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Have you had an opportunity to testify before an international court of law as to the events that took place in the former Yugoslavia or before a national court, or is this the first time you're going to testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, this is not the first time I'm testifying. I've already testified before this Tribunal and in two war crimes trials in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you've testified here already, in which case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Milutinovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you testified twice in Serbia. In which cases did you testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Podujevo case and the Skorpions case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. Please be seated. Some preliminary information as to the way the testimony is going to take place. You'll have to answer questions put to you by Ms. Dahl. I suppose you have met her as part of your preparation for this hearing. Ms. Dahl will use some time to put questions to you and she will submit documents to you. When you answer questions, please try to be specific and clear in your answers. Once this is over, Mr. Seselj, who's sitting on your left, he's the accused, he's going to put questions to you as well as part of what is termed the cross-examination. He will, therefore, ask questions of you on the topics raised during examination-in-chief. You have three Judges in front of you; at any time they're free to ask questions as per the Rules. Technically we'd rather wait until all parties have asked their questions, but sometimes when a document is submitted to all in court it may be that one of the Judges wants to put a question about it in order to avoid having to deal with it again later on in order not to waste time. We usually have breaks every hour and a half for 20 minutes for you to have a rest and also to put in new tapes. If at any time you do not feel well, don't hesitate, tell us you want to have a break. That can happen, unfortunately. If you have a question you want to put to the Bench, if you feel the need to do so, again do not hesitate to say so. So there it is. Ms. Dahl, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, have you ever served in the military?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: When did you join the military service and what service did you join?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I did my military service in 1987. That was then the JNA. I served in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: How long did you serve beginning in 1987?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: One year.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did you volunteer for military service at some point in time afterwards?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Were you in the military in 1991?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I was a volunteer.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can you describe for me how it was you decided to become a volunteer?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: In 1991 I simply decided to become a volunteer. How? Well, there were different factors influencing my decision. The political situation, the situation in society, the media. I considered that my people were under threat.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Do you -- have you ever heard speeches by Mr. Seselj during 1991?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What were the subjects of the speeches you heard from Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: In 1991, Mr. Seselj held many speeches. He held many speeches in his political career. In 1991 he explained - how can I put this briefly? - that there might again be a genocide against the Serbs. He spoke of the separation of Croatia, the status of the Serbs in Croatia. That was it in general.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Are you familiar with a concept called Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: What it is exactly, I don't know, but I do know that it was one of the standpoints in the programme of the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Where were you living in 1991?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: In Srem, the town of Sid.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did Mr. Seselj have a political party with offices in Sid in 1991?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Committees? I don't understand. In 1991 the Serbian Radical Party in Sid was set up. I don't know the date, but I know that it was founded in Milenko Petric's house.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did you learn of a call for volunteers by the Serbian Radical Party in 1991?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, but the call did not come only from the Serbian Radical Party. I did learn of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Who else gave that call?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Various politicians. Before Mr. Seselj the Serbian national interests were mentioned first by Vuk Draskovic, to the best of my recollection. He spoke of it in a different way than the Serbian Radical Party did, but he was one of those who spoke of it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: How did Mr. Seselj speak of the Serbian national interests?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean by "how."

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What did he say about them? What did he say should be done to effect them?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: What did he say? Well, everybody knows what he said. He said that the Serbs were imperilled, that the new Croatian authorities did not have good intentions as regards the Serbs, that if the Croats were leaving Yugoslavia, the Serbs in Croatia had the right to remain in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: How did you react to hearing this information?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, while I was young and went to school in Serbia, we learned a lot of things in school about World War II, about the Ustasha, about the Chetniks, although at that time we saw them as identical. The Ustasha and the Chetniks were equated by the then-communist authorities. They called them domestic traitors, but we knew quite a lot about the Ustasha crimes and atrocities. We even learned about some atrocities committed by the Chetniks. So we knew many things. As citizens --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you're now dealing with a question that I deem important. You are now speaking about the fact that Ustashas and Chetniks had been mentioned. I'd like to know this: When young people of your generation would go to school in the communist era, did you have history classes? For instance, did you have classes on what happened during the Second World War? I mean, you went to school like everybody. Can you answer this question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We learned everything about World War II and not just on the territory of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You answered my question. Thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What is meant by the term "Chetniks," from what you learned in school?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Based on what I learned in school, to say -- to speak the word "Chetnik" was prohibited in a way, as was the word "Ustasha." We learned that they were domestic traitors. In historical terms, as far as I know, in World War II the Chetniks were the Serbian royalist army under the command of Draza Mihajlovic. They were the homeland army, but the people referred to them as Chetniks and this may have been due to their methods of fighting. They were a form of guerilla, and the word "Chetnik" refers to companies, military units, and the Ustasha were in the independent state of Croatia as it was then called.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did you hear or learn from listening to Mr. Seselj's speeches a new definition of "Chetnik"?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, as I told you, in school we all learned what the Chetniks were and what the Ustasha were, but as a Serb I also heard about this from my father at home, and what he told me was not the same as what I learned in school and the same happened with the Croats. So I didn't hear anything new about the Chetniks from Mr. Seselj, but historical facts, dates, and so on, Mr. Seselj knew a lot of that better than all the rest of us did.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: And how did he describe Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Chetniks, in a word: Patriots.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Were you inspired by his view of Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, in the speeches of the time, in 1991, on Chetniks, was Mr. Seselj the only one to speak about these patriots or were there other politicians who would also speak about it? Was this a -- an issue that only Mr. Seselj dealt with: Chetniks equals patriots?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I wouldn't say that only Mr. Seselj spoke about this. Quite simply, a few years before all these events it had been a taboo topic, not to be spoken of in public. However, in 1991 the situation changed and will one could speak about this in public. No, Mr. Seselj was not the only one to speak about it. I always mention Vuk Draskovic as well because he referred to this many times. Every year they went to Ravna Gora where they erected a monument to General Draza Mihajlovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What was happening in Yugoslavia in the middle of 1991 politically in terms of the republics?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Some of the republics declared secession, first Slovenia, then Croatia, and after that Bosnia-Herzegovina too.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can you describe briefly the process of your volunteering for military service again in 1991?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I became a volunteer by applying to the Territorial Defence of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. They had an office in my town, and quite simply one afternoon I went there, I brought my personal documents, my military booklet, and I applied. On the following day they gave me weapons and two days later I was already in action attacking the village of Tovarnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did you receive any training before you were put into action?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I only checked that the weapons I was issued with were in good order.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me ask you to take a look at 65 ter Exhibit Number 32. That will show up on your screen.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see my military booklet.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can you tell me what that is.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, we call it military booklet. It's a document which every citizen of the then-Yugoslavia had to have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Dahl, you speak about document number 32. Which document is it in your folder, in your binder?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: It should be the first one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. Thank you. For it to be clear, please say that the document is the first one in the binder. It will be easier for us to follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Is the record of your service contained in the booklet?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I'd like to move this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall decide just with one decision. We're not going to give the floor to the deputy each time. We do note that you asked for this to be moved into evidence, but we will make a decision later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: How long did your status as a Territorial Defence volunteer last?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: In the Territorial Defence of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem? Usually when you just refer to the TO, then it would not refer to Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem; it would be more like the regular TO in Serbia or the Yugoslav TO. However, at that time the territory of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem established its own TO, so that's why it was called what it was. I think I remained there about two weeks, maybe even less.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Who established the TO for south-western Baranja and Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Who established it? Well, at that time there was some body in that field -- well, not in the sense of a government or I don't know what, but something like a Crisis Staff, whatever, they established it.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What coordinated the distribution of your weapons?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: You mean the first weapon I got --

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: -- as a member of the Territorial Defence? I got a weapon at a military facility in Sid. It was a temporary military facility of the Yugoslav People's Army. They gave us weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did you form into platoons and squads?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Were there other volunteers arriving in Sid to serve?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Quite a few people came, mostly from Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did the JNA have a barracks there at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: No, no, it was a civilian building that they took up, so it was a temporary facility then; but right now it is a permanent military facility.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Was there a conflict going on in Vukovar at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: At that time the conflict in Vukovar had begun. Soldiers in the barracks were under a blockade. An action was prepared for deblocking the barracks. I'm talking about those two weeks while I was among the Territorial Defence of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: You said before you went into action at the village of Tovarnik. What was the purpose of taking that village?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: What was the purpose of taking it? Well, the purpose of taking it is to take control of that area. The village of Tovarnik is very close to me. Well, the population was half-half Serb and Croat before the war. I don't know what the situation is now. Quite simply, it's on the road to Vukovar. If you want to reach Vukovar to deblock the barracks and to take the city, you have to control all the access routes to town, and Tovarnik is only the first village on that route.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, there's an item that we need to understand. While I was listening to you I was looking at your military record, your military booklet, because a military booklet is something that gives a lot of information. You know exactly what the holder did. So this concept of volunteer, I believe it's quite a problem because you go to the Territorial Defence, you show your military booklet, and at this moment did the Territorial Defence keep your military booklet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no one has the right to take away your military booklet. When you are in uniform that is the only ID you have. You're always supposed to have your military booklet on you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell me what date exactly you went to the Territorial Defence, since two days later you were in front of the village of Tovarnik. So when did you go to the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was September 1991, the beginning. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your military booklet there is a column on participation to combat. There are four entries: June 13, 1993; June 23, 1993; then April 14, 1992; April 28, 1992; then July 8, 1992; October 8, 1992; and then October 8, 1992; and December -- 9 December 1992. But there's nothing for 1991 in this military booklet. Could you please tell us why there's no mention of 1991 in this booklet?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I have the original booklet here, if I can give that to the witness so he can look through the pages you're flipping through. This bears the same evidence registration numbers that appear in the exhibit that is in electronic form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. So this is our question: Why is it that the period when you were in the TO is not on your military booklet? There's no entry of this on your military booklet.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we see in this military booklet that the person who created this military booklet created it in such a way by putting only four possibilities, four options of participating in a war. In 1991 -- well, I don't even have 1991 entered in my military booklet, like many other fields where I participated. You will see here that it is first 1993 and then 1992. I have that in different documents. This was done in a piecemeal way and, quite simply, I could have expressed my own wish and said, I don't want to have this in my military booklet, and that's it. People wanted these stamps in order to exercise certain rights in the companies where they worked and so on. So I simply have all of this on other documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll take -- please give back your military booklet and Mrs. Dahl can pursue.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: How did you end up in the unit of the Leva Supoderica?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, after the village of Tovarnik, Ilaca, and Djeletovci were taken, we were withdrawn, or rather, my platoon. Quite simply, this unit was disbanded and all the platoons were transferred to other units, and my platoon was transported to Lipovaca, picnic grounds near Sid. We had a short training course there, and from there we were sent to the Vukovar theatre of war and that is where we were attached to the Leva Supoderica Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What kind of training did you receive at Lipovaca?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, basic infantry training and drills -- well, I had already fought in those three villages, but urban warfare is a different matter, fighting in built-up areas. During the course of your military service you cannot really learn something like that. It's not like when it really happens. People who were considered experienced were brought in and they tried to explain to us how one should act while fighting in built-up areas, how to use hand-grenades, hand-held rocket-launchers, whatever.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did you learn how to communicate with civilians during combat actions?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I don't understand what kind of communication with civilians you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: If you -- were you trained how to deal with civilians you found hiding in buildings?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: We did not have any special training of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Were you given any instructions to advise them about the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, Vukovar is also a small town but with a mixed population, Serbs, Croats, Ruthenians, Slovaks lived there. So when it was being taken it had to be taken house by house quite literally because of the large-scale artillery preparations that were carried out by the JNA and of course the Croat forces were also shelling with mortars. The population was in the houses, and when we were searching the houses we had to search the basements too. You would usually stand by the windows of the basements and we would say, This is the JNA, you will be treated in accordance with all the rules. As for the Geneva Conventions, well, that was not mentioned. But at any rate, we said, According to the rules. Please come out. We will count to three or four or five, whatever people said, and then we will throw in a hand-grenade. Usually people would come out then.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Why did you tell them that you were with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, the JNA was the mainstay of everything out there, and how can I come and say, Get out, here's a Chetnik? The Croats -- all the Croats called us Chetniks, all of us, but it's logical for us to say that we are the JNA. But by virtue of the fact that I am a volunteer and a member of Leva Supoderica, I'm within the composition of the 1st Guards Brigade, I got my salary from the 1st Guards Brigade. The fact that we call ourselves Chetniks or that others call us Chetniks -- well, we're the JNA because according to our law, a reservist or a volunteer is one and the same thing. A volunteer is a person who volunteered in a unit, whereas reservists were called up. All of that was equated later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you're talking about something very important. You were talking about volunteers, but now you're saying that you were member of the 1st brigade of guards -- 1st Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So my question is simple: Were you a military man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Vukovar operations, you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Vukovar and before that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before that -- well, in Vukovar I was a member of the Leva Supoderica Detachment that was within the 1st Guards Brigade. By virtue of that fact I was a member of the 1st Guards Brigade of the JNA as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. So you were a member of the JNA in Vukovar, but before that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before that I was a member for a very brief period of time of the Territorial Defence of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, which was also under the command of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you were in military clothes, you had weapons, and you had -- you were under a military command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the unit?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Milan Lancuzanin was the commander of my unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Does he have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was called Kameni, like his father.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Do you know whether the commander had ties with the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: At the very beginning I didn't know until I was told over there. On the first or second day as we were being lined up in Nova Ulica, and that was very short, I was told that most of the volunteers were volunteers that were organized by the Serb Radical Party -- well, we were attached there to the command of the 1st Guards Brigade and we would act in a coordinated manner with them in further operations, except that we volunteers elected squad and platoon leaders amongst ourselves. We did not get any instructions from the JNA about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: How did you organize your squads and platoons of volunteers?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: In the same way like any other army. Company commander, platoon commander, every platoon had two or more squads. There were squad leaders respectively.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did the volunteers from the -- organized by the Radical Party stay together in the organizational units?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I don't understand. Are you referring to the field of Vukovar or are you speaking in general terms?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I want to focus on the individuals commanded by Kameni in the Leva Supoderica Detachment.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, in the Leva Supoderica Detachment there weren't only people from Serbia who were organized by the Serb Radical Party; there was a certain number of people who were from among the local population of Vukovar, not very many of them because usually they would belong to the Territorial Defence there but there were a number of them in our unit too. It is only logical. We needed people who were from the area itself. They were familiar with locations, with the area, and we didn't know. We were newcomers and the commander himself was a local man.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: So where did the volunteers come from if they weren't local?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, they came in groups. There was a big group of people who were from Novi Sad, the area around Novi Sad, Vojvodina, later on a group of people from Nis came and from that area, from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did you receive uniforms that had insignia and patches on them?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I personally, no, not I personally. My platoon, when it arrived in Vukovar, it was sent to Velepromet. We had lunch there and a man came there who introduced himself as the deputy commander of Leva Supoderica. He gave us camouflage uniforms and camouflage berets. As for insignia, whether they were sewn on to the uniforms, they had been sewn on to the uniforms -- I don't think there was anything on the uniforms then.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did you receive patches or did you get patches later to put on the uniforms?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: No, it was the beginning of the war. As for some organized insignia -- well, no. I personally wore a cockade but many others could wear either insignia of the Territorial Defence of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, some wore the JNA insignia, some even had the red star, five-pointed red star. There were different insignia.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did you see any insignia for the Chetnik Movement?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Insignia for the Chetnik Movement? What would that be? It would probably be the cockade.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can you explain to the judges what a cockade is?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Cockade, kokarda, well it's a symbol, or rather, it would be a coat of arms, a Serb coat of arms of the old Serbia, the Kingdom of Serbia. It was worn on uniforms or something similar to a cockade, well people tend to say that anything that looks like a cockade is a cockade, but it's very hard to explain, cockade, kokarda. Anything that was a Serb coat of arms was called cockade by people, although there are such things including two eagles or a skull and bones, different things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How was your cockade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, I had the one with the skull.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who gave you this kokarda? Did you buy it? Did you get it from the political party? Where did you obtain it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, then in 1991 it was my own. I had bought it or I had got it from someone.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: You had said that the deputy commander had distributed some camouflage uniforms. What was the name of the deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: We called him Tito. It was very hard to remember his name, but I think I managed to remember it, Zoran Ubiparipovic, but he was wounded on the very next day or the day after that in the first larger operation that we had there.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Do you know who was the commander of the Territorial Defence in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: The commander of the Territorial Defence in Vukovar was Miroljub -- Miroljub Vujovic, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did Kameni tell you who was to command the units to go into Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, we were already in Vukovar. I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What was the relationship between the detachment and the Territorial Defence in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: There was coordination, coordinated action. Even the Territorial Defence of Vukovar was under the control of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What did Kameni tell you about the -- who was the commander of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that he told me who the commander of the brigade was.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did you hear any information about Seselj's relationship to the Leva Supoderica Detachment?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, at that time we were engaged in intensive warfare, but in the evening we would sit there at the command and people did say that Vojvoda Seselj was our Commander-in-Chief, but this was -- well, it was my understanding that this was imaginary because in the field itself it was the JNA who were the commanders-in-chief. But quite simply, this was a man who organized volunteers and sent them to the theatre of war, but now this is the very beginning. If I start speaking at greater length, perhaps I may confuse things and start talking about things that happened in 1992 and things like that. Well, nothing really. He said that Mr. Seselj organized volunteers and the Serb Radical Party did too. We called ourselves Chetniks. There was also a section in the Serb Radical Party that was called the Serb Chetnik Movement, but I cannot say at that time in Vukovar whether that is the way it was all organized.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What was the purpose of the Serb fighting forces in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, what's the purpose of any army? To take control of an area, to destroy the Croat forces. At that time they were paramilitary forces as far as we were concerned. That was the objective, to destroy them and establish control over the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did you consider that you were trying to liberate the territory for Serbs?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: You see, when we take a location, a street, the Serbs who happened to be there usually joined the Territorial Defence, the TO of Vukovar. And the Croats get taken away for exchanges. I did not follow where it was that they were going. Well, some were killed, but then again that is a matter of various individuals. It is logical if the Serbs control the town that Croats would leave it, would leave the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What happened to the civilians who were leaving the town?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I personally do not know what happened, in what way they were being evacuated, whether anything had been organized. Probably that was the case when Vukovar was liberated and -- well, after two weeks it was a Serb town.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did you see civilians being mistreated?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can you describe that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, I have already said that to mistreat a civilian, that was something that the individual who found them in a basement did. There was simply evil people and they could not be controlled always. The situation could not always be under control.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What would happen when it got out of control?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, for a while they could behave inappropriately, mistreat people, even kill them, until the military police or somebody else came along. If the military police was there such things would not happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did you hear any speeches by Seselj while you were in Sid?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: More than once I listened to Mr. Seselj in Sid over an extended period of time. I don't know precisely when. I don't know the dates exactly, but once I listened to him in a sports field in Sid, later on in the centre of town, then in the premises of the Serb Radical Party in a nearby restaurant, and in Vukovar. We were sitting in a restaurant or a coffee bar belonging to Stanko Vujanovic and that is when we were celebrating the first anniversary of the fall of Vukovar. So yes, I did hear what Mr. Seselj when he made speeches if that's what you said.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me take you back in time a little bit so that we're talking about the events in Vukovar. Did you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You shall do so later on. The time has come for a break. It's 10.00. We're going to break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. I'd like address Mr. Seselj on the issue of faxes. The registrar tried to look into the matter. The problem is as follows. The fax or faxes sent by your associates are to arrive in one of the registry offices, and you said that you did not want anybody to take the documents. It is, therefore, impossible for you to move around the Tribunal premises to go and get the faxes. It looks as though the solution might be for the registry to see to it that you have available in the room where you are when you come to court to have a fax machine so that the documents can arrive on that fax and you can get them straight away. Otherwise, it's not possible for you to move about the Tribunal to go and get the faxes. So it seems from the registry that it can only be implemented as of tomorrow. Today it's impossible to get the fax machine. This is what I wanted to tell you, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm satisfied with this solution, as the OTP has announced that they will take more time to examine this witness so it's not urgent for me to receive this today, but I hope you understand that I do not trust the registry because it's evident to me that the registry has been working hand in hand with the OTP over the past five years and the former deputy registrar David Tolbert is now the Deputy Prosecutor. So as far as I'm concerned is all one and the same unit, one and the same service. I have to receive my documents in my own hands from my collaborators if they're not in The Hague, but tomorrow is not too late.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... the fax machine is available to you in that room so you can get faxes during the breaks. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, I want to go back to the formation of the unit that went into Vukovar, so let me take you back in time to September 1991 in Djeletovci. I think I've pronounced it wrong. Djeletovci. Did you meet a man there named Slobodan Medic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Who is he?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I know who he is now. If you're asking me who he was then, I don't know what you want me to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: When you met him for the first time, who did he appear to be?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: He was the commander of a unit of about 20 men. What struck me then was their equipment, their appearance. They looked very different from us. They had more expensive and better equipment and gear.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can you compare their level of training to your group?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I don't know what their training was at that time. I'm just saying that they looked more -- well, they had more expensive uniforms and vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Now, you said later you learned information about Slobodan Medic. What was that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Later on I was even a member of his unit, but in 1991, yes, I learned that he was a member, or rather, the commander of a special unit which was being formed and that they were in charge of the oil rigs in the village of Djeletovci.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Who was forming that unit?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge at the time, the first person to form that unit, to engage in forming that unit is a man whose name I can't remember right now but a high-ranking officer of the Serbian MUP known as Badza. He was in the Krajina at the time and he was in charge of forming the Territorial Defence in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Now, let me take you to a meeting you had in a restaurant in Lipovaca about the formation of the unit to go into Vukovar. Do you remember being at the restaurant hotel?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: The Lipovaca facility is a picnic ground in the Sid municipality and there is a restaurant there where we were quartered and it also had some hotel rooms at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did you receive a visit from Slobodan Grahovac, the minister of defence?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, whether he was the minister of defence, I don't know, but he was in the Ministry of Defence. He may have become minister later, but yes, his name was Slobodan Grahovac and he was with another man, I think his lasting name was Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Which minister -- or which government organization was he with?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: In the government but not the Serbian government he was there on behalf of the Territorial Defence of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem or on behalf of the district of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. They had some sort of government at the time or they were establishing one, but he was in any case a representative of that territorial district.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did he make a speech that you listened to there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, he told us that there would be a slaughter-house there, that it's not an ordinary war, that people were being killed there, that this was no military exercise, no manoeuvre. He said that whoever does not feel prepared may leave now. Well, he -- that was the gist of what he said. He said that the Ustasha forces there were very strong.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Where was he referring to when he used the term "the slaughter-house"?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: He didn't mention any place explicitly, but he was referring to Vukovar, the slaughter-house where people were being killed, that's how I understood him. That was the word he used. He said, You're going to a slaughter-house. Don't imagine you're going for a military exercise.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What did Mr. Grahovac tell you about who would be instructing you before going to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: At that time four or five men arrived. One was nicknamed Djovani and there were three or four others who were dressed in traditional Chetnik uniforms, the sort you would see in Veljko Bulajic's films. Veljko Bulajic was a film director, they had black uniforms, war beards. The main training was conducted by the man nicknamed Djovani and he was very professional.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Were they training you in traditional Chetnik weapons?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: You have to tell me what traditional Chetnik weapons are.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did they tell you stories about Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, they couldn't tell me anything I didn't know already. There was a man there called Ljuba Ivanovic. He spoke about a Chetnik code of conduct, about an oath which we never actually took, but they already had some war experience, and so did I, from the village of Tovarnik and Djeletovci, but they had, in my view at the time, more experience than I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of the other Chetnik instructors?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: We considered them to be instructors. Whether they actually were instructors, I don't know, but I remember a man nicknamed Bokal, I've forgotten his name, and another man called Milovan Tomic and several others. I may have remembered their names earlier but they escape me now. Yes, I think there was a man called Vladan Lukic or something like that. I know he was killed very early on in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Now let me turn your attention to the command post for the detachment in Vukovar for the Leva Supoderica Detachment. Did you learn about the -- how supplies were -- I'm sorry. Did you learn while you were at the command post about any relationship between the Radical Party and the Leva Supoderica Detachment?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: What I knew or heard at the time, and I heard that for the most part from a man who was I think our Chief of Staff or something like that, Slobodan Katic, and he was some sort of liaison. He travelled to Belgrade and back, but I don't know all the details precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Was Mr. Katic a member of the Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What function did he serve when he was travelling back and forth?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I can't precisely. It's possible that he was a liaison. We could ask for something as a unit, something that the radical party could organize for us or get for us through their channels. Perhaps more men. He was Chief of Staff and it was in his job description to coordinate between the army and the party. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What kinds of things did he coordinate? You mentioned men. What other -- can you give us some examples of what he did?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I can't give you examples. He didn't confide in me. We sat together in a restaurant several times in the course of the war and in my house in Sid when we were on leave for a day, but he didn't tell me specifically what his mission was. Simply, as a member of that unit, I considered him to be even deputy commander for a while because he was doing an enormous job there. But what he did precisely, I can't tell you, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did he ever give you or other members of the unit gifts from Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Not to me. I never received a gift.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did you see him deliver gifts to other people that came in the mail?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I only heard about this, that there were gifts. I don't know whether they were from Mr. Seselj or not, but the gifts were symbolic probably. I can't remember what they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did you receive a membership card in the Radical Party as part of your assignment in the Leva Supoderica Detachment?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: No, no. I only had a pass allowing me to move around during the combat operation which said that I was a member of the Leva Supoderica Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Were members of that detachment who were volunteers supposed to be members of the Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Probably, yes, they were all members and if some were not, maybe, well, they joined later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Who is Zoran Drazilovic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Zoran Drazilovic is a man who held some sort of post in the Crisis Staff of the Serbian Radical Party. I don't know much about him. I know what he looked like and I spoke to him once a very long time ago when I went out on the ground from Belgrade and I opened a file with him. He entered my name and whether I had a tour or not somewhere, identifying features if I were killed somewhere, my address. There was a photocopying shop nearby. I took -- I made a photocopy of the photo on my ID card and I gave it to him and that was the extent of my conversation with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: In this conversation with Mr. Drazilovic, were you being enrolled in something? You mentioned filling out some forms.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: The Serb Radical Party, I can't be certain but certainly they kept records. They had files on their volunteers, and he filled those files in, those cards. If you're asking me whether I was a party member at the time, I was already a member. I'm talking about my encounter with him which was official and that was in 1992 probably, not 1991. After that when that file was filled in I was sent to some barracks for brief training and after that on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Are you aware --

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: The barracks were in Bubanj Potok.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Are you aware of anyone who was kicked out of the Leva Supoderica Detachment because he did not belong to the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was not a member, but I do know that this former deputy of -- well, Ubiparipovic was accused of being a member of the SPO, the Serbian Renewal Movement, and they expelled him, they kicked him out. And the reason they gave was that he was a member of the SPO or an SPO spy or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: In connection with him being kicked out, did you see him beaten?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: As I said, they processed him physically. He was tied up, he was tied up in the basement, and it lasted a day.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: In the basement of where?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: In Kameni's house.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did you see him there tied up in the basement?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was tied to the pipes, the plumbing pipes on the ceiling.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Who tied him there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: As to who tied him, I didn't see that. When I entered the basement that's what I saw, he was already there.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Was Kameni there in the house?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: He was possibly up -- he may have been upstairs. He wasn't in the basement.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did you see anything else happen to him in connection with his processing out of the Leva Supoderica Detachment?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, there's a very banal situation. I saw him a year or two later on in company with Kameni sitting in a restaurant, that same man, which means they became reconciled afterwards probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Do you know whether Mr. Seselj was aware of the situation in Vukovar with regard to the fighting?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: He probably was. Why wouldn't he be? He visited us in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can you tell me about the -- one of the visits of Seselj when you were in Vukovar. Tell me what happened.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I know about the one visit. Quite simply, he turned up. I didn't know he was going to arrive, nobody mentioned it probably for security reasons. He simply visited us. He was taken round. It wasn't just us, members of Leva Supoderica, there were also officers from the 1st Guards Brigade who took him round to the front line, to Prvomajska street.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did he make a speech while he was touring Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: It wasn't exactly a speech. As he walked along, he spoke. He didn't stand up and hold a rally. That would have been a stupid thing to do, we could have all been killed, we were in danger from Croat mortars.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Was he addressing the soldiers around him?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj had come to visit, and of course they listened to what he said. He spoke about various matters. I can't quote everything he said.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What do you remember him talking about?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I remember that a group of men who were there in Prvomajska Street took him to show him four members of the ZNG who had been killed and three or four Croatian policemen. We had liquidated them the previous day, and I know that jokingly he said, Why don't you burn the corpses, you might catch a disease or something. Later on he tried to fire shots at a house across the road. He couldn't see any enemies there, but as a symbolic gesture he fired shots in the direction where the Croatian forces were.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did he discuss the purpose of fighting in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
