utterances.text: I don't understand what the purpose -- what you mean by that question. We all knew what the purpose was. We were there to take Vukovar. Whether he spoke about this or not, I can't say now. He said that we should be brave, that we should fight courageously, that we shouldn't allow the Croats to take control. What else could a man say who had come to visit soldiers? He came to encourage us.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did he refer to Croats by the name of Ustasha?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, we referred to them by that name as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What did Mr. Seselj say concerning Ustasha in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, what do you mean by Ustasha in Vukovar? What he said about the Ustasha in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Was he giving instructions or advice or exhortations to the soldiers fighting in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, his very arrival encouraged us. That was already something that raised our spirits. Whether he gave any advice or issued any orders, he might have done that elsewhere but he didn't do that in front of us. He might have done so when he was with the commanders somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What was the effect of his arrival on the volunteers?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I don't know how it affected the volunteers but I know how it affected me. Quite simply, I was pleased. A man had come to visit us. He wasn't afraid to come to the front line. Mr. Seselj was a political leader and we all trusted him, at least that's what I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, let me come back to a few moments ago when you showed -- or spoke about the corpses of Croats who were killed and then you said "liquidated." Could you tell me whether these people had been killed in combat or liquidated, meaning that they would have been executed once they had been made prisoner. So what did you mean exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. They were killed or liquidated in combat. That is precisely the reason. We wanted to show off in front of Mr. Seselj to commend ourselves. It would be silly to shoot anyone in front of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is the meaning you give to "liquidated"? What does it mean in your mind to be liquidated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I go into action of cleansing - that's what we call it - that's a military term, I go with the objective of preserving my own life, taking a territory, and killing or liquidating someone, whatever you call it, but not a captured man of course, in fighting, in combat. If we hadn't done it, they would have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one objection. It's probably a problem with the interpretation in different languages. In the Serbian language one can say to liquidate an enemy position, an enemy unit, a machine-gun nest, that is to say to fire in the direction of the enemy and that means liquidate. In the Serbian language liquidate does not necessarily mean to execute, shoot dead --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... the meaning given by Mr. Seselj to that notion of liquidation in your language? Does liquidating mean also that you take a position, not just -- or not executing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I meant the word "execution," I would have used the word execution; but when I used the word "liquidation," I meant precisely that, the liquidation of enemy manpower.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You took part in a military action. People were killed. I don't know in which exact circumstances they were. Therefore, I have to tell you this: When a question is put to you whose answer might incriminate you; in other words, one day it may be sort of used against you because there would be another court using this information to indict you, well, you are entitled not to answer the question because if you answered it you might incriminate yourself. But in this case the Trial Chamber might ask you to answer, all the same, and the answer you would give, as the Rules say, could not be used against you. This is what I wanted to tell you for everything to be clear. If at any time in a question put to you you sense or you think that something may be held against you, certain behaviour may be held against you, you can say, I don't want to answer this, and the Judges will see what they should do. Let us continue, Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: In answer to the Judge's question a moment ago you said that you would go into action cleansing. Can you tell me what you meant by "cleansing"?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: "Cleansing" is a military term, and it means to take a certain area in terms of expelling or destroying enemy manpower and taking that particular area. That is what cleansing means.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Do you include in that definition expelling civilians from the town?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: No. I as a soldier understand the term "cleansing" the way I described it to you a few moments ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me take you to the first day of action in Vukovar after you arrived. Do you recall what your first military objective was with Kameni?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: That should be one of those so-called mini markets that goes out into Prvomajska Street.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Were there civilians in Vukovar in the area that you were trying to take?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Were civilians detained during the engagement?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: There were civilians who were ethnic Serbs and ethnic Croats and other ethnicities, Ruthenians, Slovaks, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: So you saw civilians being detained during the military action?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I saw that, but it was I think a few days before the fall of Vukovar. I saw civilians at Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Well, let me take you to your first action in Vukovar. You told me the ethnicities of the civilians. How did you come to know what ethnic group different civilians belonged to?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: We asked them or they speak up themselves. Serbs would usually identify themselves and they would welcome us cordially, quite simple. Croats, on the other hand, looked different -- I mean, I'm not saying that they looked different physically. They looked afraid. There were cases, it wasn't only once, this happened many times, that we found in basements civilians of both ethnicities. Quite simply they would seek shelter together from artillery fire. They were separated then. I don't know. Serbs went to one place and Croats were taken to another place.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: When civilians were detained and their ethnicities checked, what happened to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I don't understand. What do you mean by "detention"? This is no detention yet. They're in, say, the yards of the private homes when they were leaving their shelters. You asked what would happen to Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me take you into your memory to being in a situation where you found some civilians who have now come out of hiding, and what I understand you to say is that at that point their ethnicity would be checked; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: And what decisions were made depending on their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I already told you, they'd be separated. The Croats would be sent in one direction, the Serbs in another, because -- I'm sorry. At that moment practically 100 per cent of the Croats wanted to be relocated to the territory of Croatia that was under Croatian control, of the Croat forces that is. Serbs, since they were from Vukovar, either went to safer places, Serbia, military-aged men would stay in the Territorial Defence. That's the way it usually was.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Were Croat civilians sent to Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that Velepromet was used as kind of a collection centre and I don't know whether it was the only such facility -- well, quite simply, I think it was a collection centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can you describe the building at Velepromet for me, please?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, the Velepromet facility is the property of a trading company in Vukovar. There are a few hangars there that are made of metal. Quite simply, they were used as warehouses for consumer goods.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Were the Croatian civilians warehoused at Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I saw them in those warehouses, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can you estimate how many people you saw?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: More than ten?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: More, more, hundreds of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: More than 500?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Madam, Madam Prosecutor, I cannot guess, but it's more than a hundred. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did you see children there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I do not recall having seen children. It is possible. If entire families were there, there must have been children there too. I personally did not see any, though. I saw the door of the hangar open and masses of people, but inside -- well, these hangars are enormous, they're not that small, and I really don't know who was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Are you aware of any civilians who were killed while they were at Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can you tell me how you became aware of killings of civilians at Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, people who are prone to do that kind of thing are prone to brag about it as well. So I did talk about a few killings that took place in Velepromet and I heard about them from a man that we call Topola.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can you describe Topola, please.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: A tall man with a beard and a strong voice and very strong physically.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did you see him committing any crime against a civilian at Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I know that he killed a man in the area around Velepromet, but I didn't see that with my very own eyes. I heard gun-shots. It wasn't that I was the only one who heard this; many of us heard this. So I cannot say with any degree of certainty whether he killed this man or not, but as I told you, this man is prone to bragging and he himself said that he had killed this person. We all believed him because that is exactly what it looked like, what he looked like.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did you see the dead body of the man you thought he had killed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, the next day by the railroad.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What did Topola tell you about having -- shooting that man?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: He tried to be ironical. It's not that he was addressing only me personally. He said that the man had tried to escape or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did he tell you something about trying to bring two presents?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes. As a matter of fact, he brought a man to the house where we were all sitting and celebrating the saint archangel. He brought a man and he brought this man, the prisoner, as a gift to the host of the patron saint's day celebration.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Who was that prisoner or that man that he brought?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, what we heard from him was that he was a member of the ZNG and he was in charge of the water-tower, so we all assumed that he had been a sniper shooter for the simple reason that the water-tower is a dominant feature there. So that was our assumption.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges what the ZNG is?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: The Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Was this man a prisoner?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, he had already been taken prisoner by someone else beforehand, but Topola brought him from Velepromet, from that collection centre. Now, whether he had stolen him from there or not, well, whether the guards knew about it or not -- but it seems that he got him from this officer of the military police that was providing security there. He said that he asked him to give him two prisoners. He killed one en route and brought the other one there.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did Topola threaten to kill the man in your presence?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: The one that he brought in? Yes, he mistreated him in different ways but he didn't kill him. Quite simply, all of that was happening in a house very close to the command of Leva Supoderica and Kameni's staff. I and another man went there and we said what was going on, but Kameni wasn't there and we said that -- there was some kind of a feast going on there. The man had not been killed yet, but it was very unpleasant. At first, perhaps since we were all a bit crazy from the war, it seemed a bit funny, but afterwards it became unpleasant. But then Kameni called one of his soldiers, Kinez, and he took him away. And a few hours later I saw Kinez and he fired a few rounds from a pistol and I asked him what he did because some people thought that he had killed the man, but he said that he fired two shots in the air in order to get people quiet because there was a lot of celebration -- there were a lot of celebrations going on on that day and I tend to believe the man because I knew him, I knew Kinez.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did you ask questions of the JNA captain concerning the two prisoners who had been taken out by Topola?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: No, I was not authorised to talk to the JNA military police captain -- well, I could talk to him, but with regard to that particular question it wasn't that I asked a question. There was a group of us there and somebody asked him about it, probably it was Kinez. But I don't remember how it was that he explained this or whether he did. I personally am not inclined to believe -- well, or rather, I am inclined to believe that he stole these two men from inside. Maybe he was assisted by someone from the inside, but I don't know. I'm simply telling you what it was that he said.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What do you recall the JNA captain's explanation to be?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I don't know what his explanation was. You know, at that time people had already known about this man, Topola, even if something had happened maybe people were afraid of him. I really cannot say anything specific.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the OTP microphone please be switched off while there is typing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, do you know what happened to this Topola?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I know is that our commander, Kameni, expelled him from the unit, although he did stay in Vukovar, nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And as far as you know, was he ever tried?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, he got killed later, so he was not tried.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Dahl, you may resume.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did you ever see Topola with a young girl in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely because of that incident Kameni -- well, I can't remember was Kameni the deputy commander of the platoon or whether he was a squad leader within that platoon. He wasn't an ordinary soldier. I mean it's not that much of a difference between a squad leader and an ordinary soldier, but I think that he disbanded that platoon and that he gave me some of the people from that platoon and others to Kinez. And as for the rest, he said, quite simply, You're no longer with us. It is precisely after this incident that this happened. And as far as I know, she ended up in a well.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can you tell me what you saw Topola doing with the girl?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: His platoon was in a house opposite the house where I had been put up. There was some mistreatment there I -- of that girl. I heard about that the previous day. I know that she was in a room but no one was allowed to enter that room, so she was in this private prison of hers for a day or two. She was accused for her husband being some kind of an extremist on the Croatian side who killed children. That is the explanation that Topola provided. I did not see her being raped by him, but everybody said that he raped her, killed her, and threw her into the well, or rather, I don't know whether he threw her into the well and thereby killed her or whether he killed her before that, before throwing her into the well.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did you see Topola leading her into the house by force?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But I saw that a day or two beforehand when I did not know at all that he had kept her as his prisoner. They were returning from an action that lasted about an hour or two, and this girl was being taken by him and his men. I was not attaching much significance to what was going on. I thought that she was taken to the command and the command to the JNA, that he would resolve it in their own way, but I did not know exactly at that first moment that he had kept her as his own prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: How old did she appear to be?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What was her ethnicity, if you could tell from her appearance?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell from someone's appearance whether he or she is a Serb or a Croat or whatever; we're all very similar. But since she had already been taken prisoner and since she was treated that way, I assumed that she wasn't a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did you make a report of what you thought Topola was doing in that house?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, otherwise Kameni would not have found out. I don't think it was only me but I think that all platoon commanders and squad leaders learned about this and reported to Kameni about it. Kameni reacted the way he did. Kameni is an energetic man, a good commander. I'm really surprised that he didn't kill him. Well, that was not practice amongst us, to have people punished that way, to have perpetrators punished that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did you go with anyone to check the house after making the report?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: We entered the house, but the girl was not there.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Who did you go with?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: With Sasa and Kinez, I think. Kinez was always there. He was -- well, we all respected that man, Predrag Milojevic. I think that he was one of the bravest members of Leva Supoderica and in a way Kameni's eyes and ears, a kind of internal control amongst us, so you could always hear something from him. So he went there to see whether it was true that the girl had been raped and whether she had really ended up in that well, and it was impossible to check that because it was a deep well.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did Slobodan Katic go into the house with you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Possibly. Right at this moment I cannot remember. It is possible. Why not? He's a member of the command.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did you find any blood in the house?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: All this is a great deal of detail. Blood was all around us, Madam. It is possible that we saw it. At any rate, as soon as Kameni resolved to expelling -- to expel him, it's obvious that there was enough proof for that. We saw him around afterwards in Vukovar, and after that I saw him in Bosnia too.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: When did you see him in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know -- well, I personally saw him in the territory of Brcko, the municipality of Brcko, he and his platoon consisting primarily of volunteers from Ruma. They had their camp there -- well, not camp. Well, they were staying at this particular place. It was a small, privately owned hotel that was called --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And before that, he had been in action in Zvornik. I was not in action in Zvornik, but the people who were there said that he was there too. That's the only thing I know. After that I heard that he got killed and I'm not quite sure that he got killed in the battle-field. I thought that he got killed in an accident in Serbia, traffic accident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you're saying that you entered the house and you don't really remember whether you were accompanied by Slobodan Katic, but you added that he was member of the command, that this Slobodan Katic was member of the command. Could you tell us exactly what you meant? What does this mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, Your Honour, if we went to check whether it was true that Topola behaved like that with that girl, that he killed her or raped her, then it's no wonder that the people who were in the command of the Leva Supoderica went to check that. If Katic was, I recall, either Chief of Staff or something very similar to that, then -- well, he was part of the command of the Leva Supoderica Detachment, so it's no wonder he was there. I don't find this detail so significant so I don't remember it. I am not sure how many people were there, who was there. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I'm supposed to understand that Slobodan Katic was part of the command structure of the Leva Supoderica unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: So let me see if I understand correctly when Topola was kicked out of the Leva Supoderica Detachment, he was transferred to another unit and you met him in that context later?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, as for his being transferred, I don't know. He probably went off on his own and applied to join another unit or he probably wandered around Vukovar with weapons. That's also a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: But when you met him in Brcko in Bosnia, he was there with another military unit?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, those are volunteers from the territory of Ruma or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did he say anything to you about Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I have already said that he was a man who liked to brag. He didn't say anything to me personally in Vukovar itself; however, in Brcko we were together on several occasions in that small hotel called Vestfalija, I can't remember exactly, and once we went to Zvornik together in a jeep on a one-day visit. And at that time he did talk about Ovcara, but at that time it was being talked about less than before. However, I did hear from him that Ovcara had happened and that he had participated in it. And there were others who mentioned Topola. He was a man not easily forgotten because of his build.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I'm sorry to ask you an obvious question, but can you tell the Judges what happened at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: All I can say is what I heard, and as the trial in Serbia is over, we now know, the Serbian public knows about this. But going back to 1991 and what I thought and knew or heard at the time, I heard that something had happened there and Kameni himself told me that something was going on there. But it was only two or three days later that I heard that there was a large-scale execution there.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: And in 1992 what did Topola say his involvement was back then?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, what could it be? If somebody participated in Ovcara, how could he have participated unless it was by killing? A man like Topola, what could his role be but to kill? And I recall him as a man who was at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I'm asking for your recollection of what he said to you, his words, what you remember.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I can't quote him now. A lot of time has elapsed since then. If I were to try to recall his words, I wouldn't be able to tell you with certainty what he said.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What's your best recollection of what you understood him to have told you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, it was an execution. Some members of the ZNG were executed there; that was my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did he tell you, I executed people?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: No, I can't say that he used those words, but in any case the way he explained it gave me to understand that he was one of the participants.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: When Topola was in Brcko, was he part of a unit that was commanded by a Vojvoda?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: What Vojvoda?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: That's my question to you. Do you know whether he was with a unit commanded by a Vojvoda?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: When he was in Brcko at the time I saw him and had contact with him, he even went into one or two operations on that territory, he was a platoon commander. Before him there was someone else but that man was killed, I didn't meet him. In those days he was the commander of those 20 or 25 men, but there was no Vojvoda.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What is a Vojvoda?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: It's a title.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: How do you become a Vojvoda?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, how do you get any title, prize? Someone has to nominate you, someone has to approve that, and then you get that title. I don't know. There were Vojvodas in Serbian history. That's a historical title. As for the present day, new Vojvodas promoted in the Serb Radical Party, it's probably because of their merits in the war, whether something they had done in military terms or organizational terms, but people were granted that title.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Who granted the title of Vojvoda within the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but to the best of my understanding it has to be another Vojvoda to propose or promote a Vojvoda. I don't know precisely how it functions, but in the Serb Radical Party the first Vojvoda was Dr. Vojislav Seselj, so it was probably at his proposal, but I can't be sure exactly how it works.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: And do you see Vojvoda Dr. Vojislav Seselj in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can you point him out, please.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: And let the record reflect that the witness has identified the accused.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Are you familiar with whether you had to have a certain number of volunteers under --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... your control --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your objection?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please tell the Prosecutor to maintain the dignity of these proceedings and pose exclusively relevant questions and not to transform these proceedings into a Serbia. It's not just all of Serbia but probably the whole world who knows that I am Vojvoda Vojislav Seselj, a Chetnik Vojvoda. There's no necessity for these theatrics in the courtroom. So could the Prosecutor please put serious questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Dahl was entitled to ask the witness whether the Vojvoda who would appoint another Vojvoda was you, and he said it was you and you confirmed this. So let's move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me return to my question. Are you familiar with whether there is a requirement to have a certain number of volunteers before one can become a Vojvoda within the Radical Party or the Chetnik Movement?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: When the Vojvodas were granted their titles, I heard earlier from Kameni that something like that was in the offing and that this was some sort of prize for their participation and their overall activity in the war. But I didn't know who the candidates were, and this was also reported in the media. I don't know whether in Serbia, but it was in Republika Srpska and I also saw these people mentioned in the newspapers who were promoted to the rank of Vojvoda.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: When you discussed this with Kameni, did he mention a figure or a number of volunteers that a Vojvoda would have -- a man would have to have under his control to become a Vojvoda?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, once you're a Vojvoda because of your wartime merits and you had been the commander of a military unit, of course you had to have a certain number of volunteers. In the Serb Radical Party there were people who were promoted to the rank of Vojvoda who did not participate in the war as such but who had assisted in other ways. So some people in the Serb Radical Party never fired shots or participated in the fighting and they were granted the title of Vojvoda all the same. So you can't really say how many men a Vojvoda had to have under his control. It depended on the terrain, on the personality count. Somebody people might prefer to be a volunteer under Kameni than someone else, so it would all depend, but there had to be a certain number of men, yes. If the man was a commander, he can't be the commander of just two or three people, me, Pero, Janko, and himself; he had to have support. He had to help the Serb Radical Party and get volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Would you agree that you would need a couple of hundred volunteers under your command?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm telling you now that I don't know precisely whether there was a kind of threshold. As a commander of volunteers, if I had less than 200, does that mean that I can or can't be a Vojvoda? I don't know. Every commander had a certain number of men depending on the situation on the ground. There were also personality cults for Vojvodas. For example, I could say, Well, I want to be commanded by Kameni and not someone who is completely unknown, and then he would have a lot of volunteers, not just members of the Serbian Radical Party but in Serbia there were many, many volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me take you back to November 1991. Did you command a platoon in the Leva Supoderica Detachment?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: When I arrived in the Leva Supoderica Detachment I was a platoon commander. Our commander, a lieutenant, went missing. We don't know to this day what happened to him. We assume he was captured and killed, and then pursuant to Kameni's orders or somebody else, somebody's orders I became a platoon commander and I remained a platoon commander until the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: And did any member of your platoon report to you that he had killed people at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, one.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: He didn't report to me, you can't say he reported to me, but he bragged about it, he spoke about it, and of course nobody believed him. Later on it turned out to be true because he has been convicted of war crimes at Ovcara in Serbia. His name was Djordje Soskic. We called him Ceca or Zorz.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What did he brag to you that he had done?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, he said silly things to me at the time, that he had cut people's throats with knives, but nobody believed him when he said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, in our platoon he was a sort of mascot. Very rarely did I approve him going into action. He probably remained in the house we used as a headquarters, as a base, and he would have hot tea or coffee waiting for us when we came back from action. So he was just a sort of janitor as far as we were concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Why did you place him in the category of a janitor or somebody who would make tea for you while you were out fighting?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, quite simply, it's not that he was actually old but he looked old. He wasn't physically fit. He was a very thin man. In our platoon there were quite a few younger men who could run and fight and we thought that he couldn't and we thought that he would be more useful to us if he met us with hot tea when we went back to the base and procured necessities for us and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Where was he from?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: From Krusevac.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Where is that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: It's a town in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Was this man a volunteer from the Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: He was a member of Leva Supoderica, but whether he was a member of the Radical Party at the time or not, whether he became a member later on, I can't say. I don't know. But he arrived there and his arrival was organized by the Serb Radical Party when they were sending volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you finally believed what he had told you about killing people at Ovcara with a knife?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: When I was partially convinced that the event at Ovcara had actually happened, I still didn't believe that he had participated in it. I thought it was an exaggeration of his because he only went into action once or twice. I didn't let him, as a platoon commander, and I thought it was just an ego trip, that he was just boasting. And then when the inspectors of the Serbian MUP invited me for an interview concerning Ovcara and put many questions to me about him, that's when I started to believe it. When it became clear to me that possibly he might have been telling the truth, and later on this was proved to be true.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: On the day of the killings at Ovcara, where were you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, I don't know on what day the murders at Ovcara took place. To this day, in spite of what it says in the media, in spite of the fact that I read about the proceedings, the trial of Kameni and others in the newspapers, I don't remember or recall the date when I heard something about it -- well, we didn't do anything. I don't remember that I did anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Do you know who -- do you know who organized the killings?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: You mean did I know then or are you asking me about what I heard and learned later on?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: As you sit here today.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, not just today but even earlier I was aware, I wasn't a hundred per cent convinced, but I think it was Miroljub who organized this.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can you give me his full name, please.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Miroljub Vujovic, the TO commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Is that the TO in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did he organize the killings with anyone else to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I don't know with who, but all the facts and everything I learned, not just I but what I heard from others, leads me to conclude that it was he who did this. I don't know why. He didn't do it on his own. He was an organizer.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did he include you in the organizing of the killing at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Me personally?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Do you know whom he invited to go out to Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether he invited anyone or not because I personally did not see or hear it, but from what was found out today, the people who were there learned that it would happen, they had to go there, and I assume it was he who organized this. And as for the people who were duty-bound to go there and carry out the task, he probably selected them himself, I don't know, but I can't really say.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm noting the time and I'm about to move into another topic, so may I suggest that we take our second break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, just a minute, before moving to something else I have a follow-up question. Witness, Soskic, nicknamed Zorz, is a member of your platoon, you're commanding this platoon and he is under your orders. You told us that this person was making coffee, tea, and was not really involved in combat action except on two occasions. This is what I would like to know. Since he's under your control, why is it that he ends up being involved in the murders at Ovcara, murders committed by the TO, according to what you said? What happened? How is it that somebody who's under your command ends up in another unit committing crimes in Ovcara? Could you tell us how this could happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, nobody from my platoon was ever worried that I was not worried if Djordje Soskic was not present at our base. He just walked around, he wandered around often, and how he went to Ovcara, who told him to go there or perhaps ordered him to go there, I might have been his platoon commander and I was, but other people could issue him with orders, also, not just me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but when later on he told you that murders had been committed in Ovcara and he took part in these crimes, as a commander yourself what did you do? You were the commander of this person.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, first of all he said that he cut people's throats there, that he killed them in a very brutal manner, so how could I believe him? I didn't believe him. Secondly, my authority was not -- it was not within my authority to conduct investigations. And thirdly, it was a taboo topic. People never spoke about it openly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I think it's time for the break. We will have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. The registrar told me that the Prosecution has already used two hours and three minutes. Please proceed, Ms. Dahl, but at this pace -- well, eight hours, that's too much for us. So you'll have to look at the timing again.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, let me bring your attention to a meeting that you had in 2003 with Kameni after arrests taken place in connection with what happened at Ovcara --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Judges, the Prosecution is not entitled to put leading questions. The right way to put this question is whether this person had a meeting at all rather than establish that there had been a meeting, and so far we have not heard the witness say that there had been a meeting of this kind at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Dahl, try to come to the question without sort of directing the witness, without putting a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I hadn't gotten to a question yet. I was trying to focus the witness's attention on time and place.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did you have a meeting in 2003 with Kameni?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't call it a meeting. But we did go to visit our fellow combatants a few times in Mitrovica, Ruma, and later on in Zemun and Belgrade. The reason was precisely the threat that there would be rest arrests. Miroljub and Stanko Vujanovic had already been arrested.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did Kameni ask to meet with you or go somewhere with you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: We lived in the same town. We saw each other every day. Yes, he asked me to go with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Who were you going to go see?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: The first time we went to Sremska Mitrovica to visit Ceca. That's a man's nickname. Later on I'm going to remember his name. At this moment I cannot. We also called him captain, who was one of the commanders during the war in Vukovar. Later on together with him we went to Ruma and saw Milojevic, Kinez.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: On the way to pick up Ceca, did Kameni talk about the investigation of Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes. We all knew about that already. He personally had not been summoned yet. Later on he was summoned to the MUP premises for an interview. At that time he hadn't been and he doubted whether he would be called.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What did you understand the purpose of the four of you getting together during the investigation of Ovcara to be?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, the purpose was simple, to talk about that and in a way, agree on how in case you were interviewed by the MUP you would answer. Well, in order to have an answer. Quite simply, I -- no, I was not at Ovcara but I was accompanying Kameni during the year before that, certainly. Kameni's a very sick man and it was always good for someone to be with him. Amongst themselves, they were trying to reach agreement on this and they were discussing this.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Between 2002 and 2003 did you travel with Kameni?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did you assist him in driving to pick up Ceca?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: No, Ceca was driving.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: And after you -- after Ceca joined you, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: To Ruma.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: It's very nearby, it's the next town.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: In Ruma where did you go?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: We stayed in Ruma. We went to a restaurant near the railway station.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Before going to the restaurant at the railway station, did you pick up Kinez?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember whether he came on his own or whether Kameni or Ceca had informed him by mobile phone -- at any rate, he doesn't live far away from the railway station.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: How did the conversation start about what to say if there were questions about Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: They were reaching a very simple agreement. I don't know whether Ceca, but Kinez and Kameni at one point were at Ovcara and they did see something there. So they were trying to reach agreement as to what was necessary and how to behave in case there were to be an investigation. At that moment, they did not know whether they were involved in the investigation or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did Kameni express concern about who might be prosecuted for what happened at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, no. For himself he never -- well, he was not afraid personally. On the basis of all my socialising with him I understood, and I'm practically convinced that he had not killed anyone there, but quite simply the man was concerned, he was worried. Until you prove that, you can spend a certain amount of time in detention or whatever. Quite simply, the man was worried.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Where did he think the prosecutions would be held?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Serbia, Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did he fashion a factual scenario that he thought would provide him with a defence?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, he -- well, not he but they together reached this agreement or, simply, they were recounting what it was that had happened there in order to remember all of this in case of an investigation. I remember that Ceca insisted that no one should mention JNA members being there at any point in time. I don't know, but he simply insisted on that. All the rest is the way they had put it there, and I remember that the defence in the court in Belgrade was like that. The judgement pertaining to Kameni states that he did not personally take part in the liquidations, but that he was around. I don't know about the others. I did not follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you're now speaking about the judgement in Belgrade. I'm not aware of it. I don't have it. But I'm trying to sort of shed some light. All this is very complicated indeed. Kameni is, indeed, Milan Lancuzanin. Was he acquitted by the Belgrade court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, he was convicted to a maximum sentence at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So he was convicted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did Kameni discuss the people who had been indicted in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: No. There was this case that was now brought to an end. Major Sljivancanin, that case, he talked about the Sljivancanin and Radic case.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Well, how did he think he could protect himself from guilt?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: He did not say that he could protect himself from guilt, or rather, who? Who would protect himself from guilt?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Well, I'm trying to understand the conversation. You told me that they began talking about what to say if they were contacted by the MUP investigators.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can you summarize what story they fashioned on that day?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether the story was made up or whether it's simply a compilation of what happened there, but I can tell you what the conclusion was that they reached, how it was that they were supposed to speak in case there were to be an investigation. Very briefly, they were in Belgrade on that day, which is certain. I mean I'm almost certain that Kameni was in Belgrade on that day. That happened in the evening hours. They came from Belgrade. They find out that Miroljub is urgently asking to see them, that he's -- or rather, Kameni heard that Miroljub was looking for him and that he was asking for them to meet at Ovcara. And Kameni went there with his escorts to Ovcara. He sees there that what was being prepared was a liquidation. Kameni even tried to help someone there, a man there, but he did not succeed in that. In the stage when people were being transferred to some vehicles and taken further away, I don't know whether these vehicles were tractors or whatever, I can't remember now, Kameni ordered that they be returned from Ovcara and go to their base in my street. It was something along those lines. Yes, at the moment when Kameni left, Vujovic stops him and says, You're not going to leave me now, are you? And then he answered, That's not my job. And then he leaves. That is roughly how they summarized what it was that was going on. Earlier on, too, earlier on Kameni presented this identical version not only to me but to other people too, something very similar to that much earlier in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: When you were listening to their conversation, could you tell whether they were talking about facts or making them up?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. It's certain that there is something there, but was it because they forgot or was it because they were making things up? I don't know. Not at a single moment did they say that they were guilty, that they had killed anyone there. Quite simply, it seemed as if they were jogging each other's memory. One would say, Do you remember this? And the other would say, Well, no, don't you remember that it was something else. It was along those lines. Finally they came to a conclusion. They put together a picture, so to speak, regarding all of this, and then they agreed that that is what they would say. I cannot know whether that is the truth, partly the truth -- well, quite simply, I wasn't there and in their conversation not at any point in time could you get the impression that they were speaking in the context of the actual perpetrators. No. That was not being referred to. Now, was it because of my presence or not, but I don't believe that it's because of my presence. At any rate, it is many years afterwards and even if someone were a murderer, if he had any sense left, he would not admit to that when judicial proceedings were already being prepared.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did they discuss with you whether or not to -- I'm sorry, did they discuss in front of you whether they should tell the truth if there was an investigation by the Serbian judiciary or the Hague Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Whether they came to the conclusion that they should tell the truth, is that what you're asking?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did they discuss whether or not they should tell the truth when questioned?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: No, they said that that's the only truth. Kameni even repeated that, what they agreed upon -- well, all the things they heard, that that is the only truth, that that is the way we should defend ourselves if any one of us were to be investigated. They still thought that they would not be accused, not any one of them, they simply thought that they could be interviewed in investigation proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did Ceca discuss how to minimise JNA involvement?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Ceca who? Ceca who?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Ceca who was in the meeting with you at the restaurant, at the railway station.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Oh, Ceca, you mean. Ceca spoke about it -- well, he's a man who exceptionally likes and respects Major Sljivancanin, and he told us then that he is often in touch with him over the telephone and they would even see each other at military hotels while he was still in hiding. And I know 100 per cent sure that they were close, that they socialised after the war, Ceca and he.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did he say in front of you that they should try to minimise the JNA involvement by saying they saw only uniforms of the Vukovar Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: He said that the JNA should not be involved in any of this in any way, not to diminish their presence or whatever, that they should not say that JNA uniforms were seen there. That is what he was saying to Kameni, something along those lines, because he was afraid that Major Sljivancanin could be convicted here.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did you make any suggestions about uniforms?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: No -- well, I did say that we were all in JNA uniforms and that it would be silly to say that we didn't say -- that we didn't see JNA uniforms when we wore them ourselves, JNA uniforms. I mean, from 5 or 10 metres away you could not distinguish different uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What was Kinez's reaction to your comments about what to say about uniforms?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Kinez, Kinez -- I mean Ceca and Kameni had their own version of the event and Kameni had his own. And conditionally speaking, it was Kameni's version that was adopted. But I had heard it earlier on. It wasn't that Kameni said anything new then. In 1991 he said that he saw it that way, along similar lines. He never denied that he had been at Ovcara. He never participated in that massacre. He never said that he did anything there. Many years later as well -- well, I personally think that he didn't, he, he, we are talking about him, the man, the person.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did Kameni suggest that he and others were all at the SRS Main Staff in Belgrade that day?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, now I'm not sure whether it was at the Serb Radical Party in Belgrade, but I am convinced that it was in Belgrade. Well, why not at the premises of the Serb Radical Party in Belgrade? Well, at this moment I cannot recall. Maybe I will remember later. He didn't insist on that detail. Quite simply, Belgrade was Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Do you know whether -- as you sit here today remembering the events, what you saw of Kameni on the day of the massacre at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I never can say on what day the massacre at Ovcara was committed. I cannot say the exact day, but when something happened in Ovcara in the evening, Kameni said that all platoon commanders should check the number of personnel in their platoons.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I did that, but that was nothing new. We often did that if the commander asked us to check the personnel level. Yes, I did that. A few of my people were missing, but it's not that it was serious -- well, except for a few that had taken their regular leave, gone home. If people were not in action for a couple of days, well, they were prone to loitering about.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: So did you -- do you know whether or not Kameni was absent that day or not?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: He himself said that he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: When Kameni established the factual situation, did they agree that they would tell anybody else what their version of the facts was?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I don't know. No one ever publicly lined up the unit and said such and such a thing happened or such and such a thing did not happen. Quite simply, in the command the commander said that strange things were going on. I cannot use his exact word now, but he said that what was going on there was not a good thing. And then he asked for the personnel level and then we all went to handle that, and then we returned to the command and said what the respective personnel levels were. But basically what he said was that bad things were happening at Ovcara. He wasn't speaking in literal terms, that there was killing going on there, something like that. It is only that word went from mouth-to-mouth a few days later.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: In 2003 when you are meeting with Kameni and Ceca and Kinez, did Kameni tell you something about trying to release a prisoner?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: He didn't speak to me. He was speaking to everyone. I think that he did mention that event, that he tried. Now, was this an acquaintance of his or not, I don't know. It wouldn't be surprising if it were his acquaintance because, after all, Kameni was born in Vukovar, lived there all his life. After all, they were a reputable family, they were carpenters, they had their own company.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: So what story did he give you about trying to save a prisoner or mention in front of you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, he saw a man there who had been taken prisoner. He tried to take him away from there. That's what he said, but Miroljub didn't allow it. That is literally that.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did he tell you what he replied when the prisoner asked for help?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I said that the prisoner asking for help, most probably he recognised the prisoner and tried to help him.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I'm asking what you remember of what Kameni told you or said in front of you when you in 2003 were meeting with Ceca and Kinez and Kameni?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: He said that if there was an investigation, that was a detail that had to be mentioned. I don't doubt that he tried to assist someone there. That's what he said to Ceca, If they question, you mention that detail also, don't let there be accusations only, let it also be said that we tried to help someone.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did Ceca try to call Sljivancanin during that meeting?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Not Sljivancanin. He tried to contact him but he said he was unable to establish contact with him right away. He did it through someone and an hour later Sljivancanin himself called him, but it didn't happen while we were sitting there.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What didn't happen, the call back or --

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes. The call back did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: When the meeting concluded, was there any indication on whether they were going to share the story with other people who might be involved?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether they told that to anyone else. We also went to Zemun and saw some people there and it was always the same story, in essence. Whether each of them separately then retold the story to others, I don't know. It didn't seem to be an order issued by Kameni. He was no longer the commander anyway. It was simply people who knew each other, Ceca, Kinez, myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did there come a point in time where Kameni was interviewed by the Belgrade MUP?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: That was a special MUP unit for investigating war crimes, but it wasn't in Belgrade. They came to Sid, and then over a three-day period they interviewed many people in Sid, including Bora Bogunovic, Kameni, and myself very briefly. Kinez was taken to Belgrade to take a lie detector test, and after that, he was released. He came back to Sid right away. He told us that he had been tested with a lie detector and that everything was all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You say that as part of the investigation, the MUP uses lie detector tests?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but Milojevic was the one. Kameni didn't say that he had taken a lie detector test.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: But when you met with -- I'm sorry, did you meet with Kameni and his lawyer after Kameni's interview?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: He wasn't his lawyer yet, but Kameni wanted to engage him for the simple reason that he was already afraid. It's always better, even in the investigation phase, to have a lawyer working for you for the simple reason that Kameni can't concentrate very well. He's suffered two or three strokes, and he didn't want to make any statements without the presence of a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did Kameni tell you about the interview he had with investigators from The Hague Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes. He offered me a video which I didn't want to view. He told me that his entire interview was there, and he took his lawyer along for that too. He didn't go to meet The Hague investigators without his lawyer. He returned home. We went to have a coffee together, and he said that there were audio and video recordings of that interview and they gave him a cassette at his insistence.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did Kameni tell you anything about what to say if you were contacted by investigators about Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: No, no one involved me in that. I wasn't there. It was more an agreement among the people who had been at Ovcara at a certain point in time. I was not in Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did the lawyer tell people present at that meeting to forget about it like it never happened?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Judge, such questions can't be asked. The question could be: What did the lawyer say, not whether the lawyer said this or that. It's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're right. Mr. Seselj is right. Please rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did the lawyer give any instructions about how to address questions about the events at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Quite simply, he said at the end, Just go home quietly, don't be afraid, just forget it ever happened as if it had never been, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did Kameni give any instructions about using cellular telephones to contact each other?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: We took the batteries out of the mobile phones during the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What was the effect of removing the batteries?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. There's a belief, I don't know whether technically that's how it is or not, that if you do that, no one can listen in, no intelligence services can listen in. I don't know if that's true or not, but I did remove the battery from my phone.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Was it an attempt to keep anybody from listening to your conversations?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes. You know what? People were afraid. If there was an investigation, they thought someone might be listening in, might be bugging certain persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: So is it your testimony today that you left the meeting with Kameni and Ceca and Kinez with the impression that they had gotten together to refresh each other's memories and tell a truthful, consistent story?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: They did refresh each other's memory and fill in the gaps in each other's stories, but whether what you say is true, I can't say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: So you didn't consider they were making an attempt to cover up their role in the Ovcara massacre?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, if they did have a role in the Ovcara massacre they didn't discuss it in front of me or probably in front of anyone. So no one could conclude that they actually did participate in the massacre. Quite simply, they were there. It turns out they were witnesses, and it was not my conclusion that that was what they were actually doing, that that was the gist of their conversation. The conversation was conducted in such a manner that they were simply filling in the gaps in each other's recollections. I didn't have the impression that they were trying to cover up their personal participation, at least they didn't mention anything like that. If one of them had said, You know, we're not going to say we killed this one or that one, let's say something else, they didn't say that. They never mentioned murders. They saw it as a problem, but either they were innocent or they were afraid someone was listening in. There can be various reasons.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: But you were listening in, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: And there were points in the conversation where it got hot, yes?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: And those were the points where they began to omit personal involvement when they were discussing things in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Judges, this is again a leading question. The Prosecutor has no right to put such questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Dahl, it is true that the way you phrased your question was a bit suggestive, leading. Could you please reformulate your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honour, I need to get a clear answer before I confront Mr. Stoparic with his signed statement to the contrary. So if I can beg your indulgence and get either a yes or no, and I can ask Mr. Stoparic to look at his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we have here some matter of procedure. This is a viva voce testimony. This is not 92 ter, so theoretically, the written statement does not need to be produced or presented unless you decide that you need to refresh his memory because on one point in the written statement that you have he is being evasive. Then show him the written statement according to the rules of the Appeals Chamber just to refresh his memory, saying, This is what you said earlier and now I will show you the written statement where you say something -- some other thing. You come from the common-law system. You know exactly what I'm hinting at.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So please follow the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Do you recall whether there were points during the conversation that it appeared to get hot when the conversation touched on the personal involvement of the participants in the Ovcara massacre?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object again. The question could be, Were there stages where the conversation became hot? Not whether, Do you recall whether this happened? The Prosecutor can say whether any points where the conversation became hot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Dahl, please rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I need to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As -- since there's some problems, maybe I will ask the question myself. Witness, you were having a conversation with people who, rightfully or wrongfully, believe that maybe one day they might be heard by an investigating judge in Serbia. This is a meeting which you attend, and the discussion is on what might have happened at Ovcara. According to your recollection, what were the position of each and everyone in relation to what had happened at Ovcara? Could you say exactly what each and everyone said regarding this, and then we will continue on with other questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour. I did not participate in the conversation. I spoke up very little. Kameni was very calm, but Ceca said to Kinez very often, Keep quiet, you know nothing about it. Or, The other way around. The two of them spoke more loudly and they often contradicted each other about various points. Kameni was the only one who was calm throughout the conversation. If that's what you are referring to in your questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Something's up, there's four of you, yourself, Kameni, Ceca, and Kinez. According to what you're saying, you're in the background and not really taking part in the conversation. Kameni is still -- is very quiet, but it seems that there is tension between Ceca and Kinez.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. According to you, what is the reason for this tension?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite simply, for example, Kinez would start a sentence and Ceca would interrupt him and stop him from completing it. So Kinez never managed to complete his sentence so I couldn't tell you what he intended to say. They knew each other better than I knew either one of them. They had spent more time in each other's company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, starting from this foundation, Mrs. Dahl, could you please continue. We could probably save time if I was asking the questions, but this is not provided for in the Rules.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me go back to when you got involved in the conversation. Did you make a suggestion about whether the group should acknowledge wearing JNA uniforms?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've already said. It's absurd to say that I didn't see any JNA uniforms there when we ourselves were wearing JNA uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did Kinez reply to you when you made that suggestion?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, he might have said, Shut up, you fool, or something like that. I can't remember right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me show you your statement to refresh your recollection.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: In e-court document 07044.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me ask you to look at paragraph 152.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, we need to have paragraph 152 in English and 152 in the -- in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: In Serbian the paragraph is located at page 36, the internal page number of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have paragraph 152 in Serbian and 152 in English. The best would be to have both paragraphs side by side, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can you review paragraph 152 to see if it refreshes your recollection about what Kinez said to you when you involved yourself in the conversation.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, I've answered that. It's precisely what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, Witness, please read this paragraph in your language out loud, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "That was the first time I got involved in the conversation. I said that we, that is, the members of the 'Leva Supoderica' Detachment wore new JNA camouflage uniforms that we received at the 'Velepromet' facility in Vukovar. 'Kinez' said to me that I should shut up and be happy because I wasn't there." Well, that's precisely what I said, Kinez told me to shut up -- well, it says here he told me to be glad I hadn't been there, well, quite simply, I could not be a subject of investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I need to make a request for an interpreter's clarification. You asked the witness to read and in the English the words "we would say" were omitted from the interpretation from the second sentence that begins: " ... I said that we would say that the members ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll do this once again. Please read this paragraph again out loud slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "That was the first time I got involved in the conversation. I said that we, that is, the members of the 'Leva Supoderica' Detachment wore new JNA camouflage uniforms that we received at the 'Velepromet' facility in Vukovar. 'Kinez' said to me that I should shut up and by happy because I wasn't there." That's what it says here. Probably it wasn't what he said. He probably said I should be glad that I hadn't been there.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Does that refresh your recollection about what Kinez said?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, that's what I said previously. I, quite simply, didn't recall that he said I should be glad I hadn't been there. But even before I read this out aloud, I told you all this.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please. When you're saying that he should be glad I hadn't been there, means not be at Velepromet, is that it? You should be happy not to have been in Ovcara, not to have not been at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He meant to say I should be glad I hadn't been at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did you understand that the people in the conversation that day were making an agreement about what they would say to investigators if they were questioned?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, of course. They were agreeing as to how they should conduct themselves if they were interviewed about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did they agree on a factual situation that was different from what you personally observed when you were in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Previously Kameni had said something similar to this, not only to me but to others, as early as 1991. But I have no way of knowing whether it was to distract attention from the actual events or not because I myself was not an eye-witness of the events at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, I want to repeat my question. Did the factual scenario they agreed upon that day differ from what you personally observed at Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm telling you, I couldn't observe anything at Ovcara personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did you observe whether or not Kameni was there or in Belgrade at the particular points in time that we're discussing?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Kameni says he was in Belgrade in the morning. You see, to go from Belgrade to Vukovar by car it takes two and a half hours or even less if you have a good car. In wartime the motorway was empty, there was no traffic, so you could get there even faster.
